name: Aisha Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office at an architecture practice, about twenty-five people, two floors above a bakery. My day is the partners' diaries, client meeting bookings, invoicing support, planning application paperwork and keeping the model-making room from turning into a tip. I'm the person everyone asks where things are. I love it when a big submission goes out on time because I chased every signature.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Architects who think deadlines are suggestions. I once spent a whole Friday evening getting wet signatures from a client in a car park because someone forgot. I also get tired of being the only one who knows how the printer contract works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd probably make a joke about it in the office group chat. I use the AI for drafting the odd email and it's fine. The AI doesn't know which client hates being called before ten. I'd say the job's about knowing people, and that hasn't changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty secure. The practice is busy, I've had two pay rises in three years, and the partners rely on me. My only real money worry is my rent, which is most of my pay, but I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep using AI for the boring email drafts. I'd keep putting a bit aside each month for a deposit, maybe in three or four years. I might also finally do the project coordination course the practice keeps offering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Life carries on and I like my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that could still go wrong for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice losing a big client, honestly. We had a scare last year when a developer pulled out of a housing scheme. If that happens again, they'd cut freelancers first, and I'm pretty central, so I'd probably be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you rely on outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Noor, who's a primary school teacher, and my mum, who rings every Sunday. Noor and I split everything down the middle. If something went wrong, I'd go back to Mum's for a bit, which I'd hate but could do.

say: I'd joke in the office chat that the **AI hype** fizzled, which I half expected.
I'd say admin is about **knowing people**, like which client hates early calls.
think: I feel **secure**, with two pay rises and partners who rely on me.
My one money worry is **rent**, but four months' savings covers a shock.
do: Keep using AI for **boring email drafts** and nothing more.
Keep putting money aside for a **deposit** in three or four years.
Finally sign up for the practice's **project coordination** course.
feel: **Calm** and content, because she likes her life as it is.
S0.quote: The AI doesn't know which client hates being called before ten.
fieldNote: She's a **light user** of AI and sees it as a helper, not a threat, here.
Her security rests on the practice's **client pipeline**, which she watches closely.
She has a clear **fallback** in her mum's house, which lowers her stress.

steps.text: Keep using AI only for routine email drafts
Put aside money each month for a flat deposit
Sign up for the practice's project coordination course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that firms need to share the gains with staff, not just cut heads. I'd post about a four-day week, because if software does half the admin, people should get time back. I'd also say there should be rules on what bosses can automate without consulting people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. Booking, invoicing support and chasing paperwork is exactly what the card lists, and a lot of my week is that. I think the partners would keep me but not hire the junior we'd planned, and my job would turn into managing the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools the practice brings in, because I'd rather be the one running them. I'd ask the partners for a new job title and a written role, something like operations coordinator, so it's clear I'm more than bookings. And I'd save a bit harder, an extra hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd feel like I had to prove myself again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be running the tools that shrink admin. Does that sit right with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, no. I'd feel a bit of a hypocrite pushing for rules online while setting up the software at work. But refusing wouldn't stop it happening, and at least I'd make sure the junior role becomes something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the partners would you go to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen, who hired me. She's practical and she hates waste, so I'd pitch it as saving her money while keeping someone who knows the clients. I'd have the new role written out on one page before I walk in.

say: I'd say firms must **share the gains** with staff, not just cut heads.
I'd post in favour of a **four-day week** and rules on automating without consultation.
think: Booking, invoicing and paperwork chasing is **exactly** what the card lists.
The partners would keep me but drop the **planned junior**, and I'd manage software.
do: Become the practice's **best user** of whatever tools come in.
Ask partner Helen for a written **operations coordinator** role.
Save an extra **hundred** a month on top of the usual.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, with a sense that she has to **prove herself** again.
S1.quote: I'd feel a bit of a hypocrite pushing for rules online while setting up the software at work.
fieldNote: She names her own **contradiction** before I could raise it.
Her plan is to **reshape** her role on paper rather than wait to be reshaped.
She sees the cost landing on the **junior** who never gets hired.

steps.text: Learn the practice's new booking and invoicing tools first
Pitch Helen a one-page operations coordinator role
Save an extra hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government response like a pandemic, emergency income, fast. I'd be signing everything and probably marching. I'd say it's not the workers' fault and we shouldn't be the ones who pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of a job by 2028 or soon after. Everything I do is thinking work, and if AI can do planning applications and invoicing as well as me, the partners won't pay my salary. The architects themselves would be in trouble too, so the whole practice might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd pull every penny I can into savings and stop the deposit dream. I'd look hard at hands-on work, since robots are about three years behind, maybe training as a dental nurse like my cousin. I'd also talk to Noor about moving somewhere cheaper together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. My stomach drops just picturing the partners' meeting where they tell us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Lara does it and says it's busy, physical and nobody wants a robot in their mouth. It's a two-year course, so I'd finish around the time AGI lands. It's three years more than I'd have in an office, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum on the Sunday call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I might need her spare room for a bit, and that I'm sorry. She'd say of course, and then she'd worry quietly for a month. I'd hate that more than the job.

say: I'd call for an **emergency income** scheme, like during a pandemic.
I'd say **workers** shouldn't pay for this and I'd probably march.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2028 or soon after.
If the **architects** are in trouble too, the whole practice shrinks.
do: Drop the **deposit plan** and pull every penny into savings.
Look into a two-year **dental nurse** course to buy time before robots.
Talk to Noor about **moving somewhere cheaper** together.
feel: **Frightened**, with her stomach dropping at the thought of the **partners' meeting**.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum I might need her spare room for a bit, and that I'm sorry.
fieldNote: She grasps that her job is **all thinking work**, so the robot gap doesn't protect it.
Her retraining idea comes from a **cousin's** real job, which makes it concrete.
The thought of **worrying her mum** hurts her more than losing the job.

steps.text: Stop saving for a deposit and build emergency savings instead
Enrol on a two-year dental nurse course
Find a cheaper flat with Noor
Sign petitions and join marches for emergency income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so unions, firms and government should be planning together now. I'd push for the practice to pay for staff retraining before it happens, not after. Online I'd be the annoying one sharing reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is just enough for me to switch, if I start straight away. My job still goes, but I'd be thirty-two and in a new career, not starting from zero at thirty. That's a real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in the first year, either dental nursing or something in health admin with patients face to face. I'd keep working at the practice while I study, because the pay matters. I'd keep the deposit savings but pause adding to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a plan in it. I can breathe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the partners you're retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first. Helen's good, but I wouldn't want them to plan around me leaving. I'd tell them once I had a place sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The submissions going out, honestly, and the buzz in the office on a deadline day. I'm good at that, and starting as a trainee somewhere would sting. But I'd rather be a beginner at twenty-nine than redundant at thirty-one.

say: I'd say **unions, firms and government** should plan together now.
I'd push the practice to pay for **retraining** before AGI lands, not after.
think: Five years is **just enough** to switch if I start straight away.
I'd be **thirty-two** in a new career, not starting from zero.
do: Start a **part-time course** in dental nursing or patient-facing health work.
Keep working at the practice while studying, because the **pay matters**.
Pause adding to the **deposit savings** but keep what's there.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to **breathe** because there's a plan.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a beginner at twenty-nine than redundant at thirty-one.
fieldNote: The extra three years turns **fear into a timetable** for her.
She'd keep her retraining **quiet** at work, a gap between public and private.
She'll miss the **deadline buzz**, which is where her pride sits.

steps.text: Start a part-time dental nursing or patient-facing health course
Keep working at the practice while studying
Pause deposit savings but keep the money already there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so let's use it for proper public retraining, not just wait. I'd say it at work, and I'd probably get involved with a campaign for it. I'd also say architects need to think hard about what they'll still be for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel I'd be all right. Ten years is a whole career stage, and I'd have time to move into something with people and hands. My job goes eventually, but not in a way that wrecks me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the project coordination course this year, then look at health or care work over the next few years. I'd keep saving for the deposit, because I might still buy before 2036. I'd use the AI tools more in the meantime so I stay useful at the practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools more. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever the practice brings in for invoicing and planning paperwork, plus the chat tool I already use for emails. I'd start using it for the meeting minutes too. If I'm going to leave in five years, I want to leave as the person who knew the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd actually buy a flat with Noor, or with whoever I'm with by then. I'd probably still wait a couple of years to see which way it's going. I don't want a mortgage I can't pay in 2037.

say: I'd call a decade a **gift** and push for proper **public retraining**.
I'd say architects should think hard about what they'll **still be for**.
think: Ten years is a whole **career stage**, enough to move into work with people.
My job goes eventually, but **not in a way** that wrecks me.
do: Take the **project coordination** course this year.
Use the practice's AI tools more, including for **meeting minutes**.
Keep saving for a **deposit** but wait a couple of years before buying.
S4.quote: I don't want a mortgage I can't pay in 2037.
fieldNote: With a decade, she moves from **defence** to planning.
She'd become a **stronger AI user** to leave on a high, a steady adopter's choice.
Her **housing plans** are the clearest sign of how warning time changes things.

steps.text: Take the practice's project coordination course this year
Use AI tools for invoicing, planning paperwork and minutes
Keep saving for a deposit and delay buying a couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything except panic. What would help is government paying people while they retrain, properly, not a token course. And firms like ours being made to give notice and training money before cutting staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the juniors. I got my start because someone gave me a junior admin job at twenty-two. If those first jobs vanish, the next lot of people like me never get on the ladder at all.

headlineQuote: If those first jobs vanish, the next lot of people like me never get on the ladder at all.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** office lead at an architecture practice, the person who **chases every signature**.
She's **progressive**, wants firms to share gains, and admits being a **hypocrite** about running the tools.
She uses AI **now and then** and would learn more once her practice adopts it.
She's **calm** in AI Plateau and **alarmed** under fast AGI, steadied by time to retrain.
Her fallback is her **mum's spare room**, and her worry runs to the **juniors** who come after her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to do anything except **panic**.
whatWouldHelp: Government **paying people** while they retrain, and firms giving notice and **training money** before cuts.
